what_its_for: Neratinib is a cancer medicine used to treat HER2-positive breast cancer. It is used after you have already finished treatment with another medicine called trastuzumab (Herceptin). It helps stop cancer cells from growing and spreading by blocking certain proteins that cancer cells need to survive.
how_to_take: Take neratinib by mouth with food every day. Swallow the tablets whole — do not crush, chew, or split them. Try to take it at the same time each day. It is very important to also take an anti-diarrhea medicine called loperamide (Imodium) during the first few months of treatment, as directed by your doctor, to help prevent or reduce diarrhea.
dosing: The usual dose is 6 tablets (240 mg total) taken once a day with food. Always take exactly the dose your doctor prescribes. Do not change your dose on your own. Your doctor may lower your dose if you have side effects.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, skip the missed dose and take your next dose at the regular time the following day. Do not take two doses on the same day to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store neratinib at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Keep the bottle tightly closed and store it out of reach of children and pets.
what_to_avoid: Avoid grapefruit, grapefruit juice, and Seville oranges (sometimes found in marmalades), as they can increase the amount of this medicine in your blood and raise your risk of side effects. Avoid taking antacids that contain magnesium, calcium, or aluminum within 3 hours before or after taking neratinib, as they can make the medicine less effective. Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take, as many drugs can interact with neratinib. Avoid becoming pregnant while taking this medicine, as it can harm an unborn baby.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: severe or ongoing diarrhea (especially more than 5 loose stools per day), signs of liver problems such as yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice), dark urine, severe stomach pain, or extreme tiredness, nausea or vomiting that prevents you from eating or drinking, signs of dehydration such as feeling dizzy, very thirsty, or urinating very little, sores in your mouth that make it hard to eat or drink, severe skin rash or peeling, or any unusual symptoms that worry you.
when_it_works: Neratinib starts working right away at the cellular level, but you may not feel a difference. This medicine is taken to help reduce the chance of your breast cancer coming back after your previous treatment. Your doctor will monitor your progress with regular check-ups and lab tests. It is important to keep taking it as prescribed for the full course of treatment, even if you feel well.
special_populations: Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do not use neratinib if you are pregnant, as it can harm your unborn baby. Women who can become pregnant should use effective birth control during treatment and for at least 1 month after the last dose. Men with female partners who can become pregnant should also use birth control during treatment and for 3 months after. Do not breastfeed while taking neratinib and for at least 1 month after your last dose. Liver problems: If you have liver disease, tell your doctor before starting this medicine, as your dose may need to be adjusted or this medicine may not be right for you. Older adults and children: This medicine is not approved for use in children. Older adults can take it, but should be monitored carefully for side effects.
